Concentration: Global Africa and the Diaspora, Gender, Sexuality and Women's Studies, Urban Studies, Law and Society
Description: The Africana Studies major is an interdisciplinary major in the humanities and social sciences that is designed to provide students with an understanding of the history, culture, and social realities of people of African descent. Majors in Africana Studies are expected to develop a sophisticated understanding of the theoretical and methodological issues that inform the field. They are also expected to demonstrate a solid familiarity with the key historical moments, intellectual movements, and social struggles that have shaped the discipline. The Africana Studies major requires a minimum of 14 course units. We encourage students to double-major, as Africana Studies provides a unique perspective to students who major in other disciplines, from English to Economics, and from Psychology to Biology.

Requirements: Prospective students must apply using the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application must include the Penn-specific Supplement with its required essays, an official high school transcript, a School Report, one letter of recommendation from a school counselor, and two letters of recommendation from teachers. Standardized test scores (either SAT or ACT) are also required. Reports such as the Mid-Year Report and Final Report are required when available.
Concentration: ['Greek and Roman history', 'Near Eastern history']
Description: The major in ancient history is an interdisciplinary major, sponsored by the Departments of Classical Studies and History. All majors are assigned an advisor from one of the two departments and should consult with their advisor on a regular basis. The major is an appropriate background for many fields and professions, including law and medicine, and for graduate work in history, classics, archaeology, and other related disciplines. There are two concentrations, one in Greek and Roman history, the other in Near Eastern history.

Concentration: Archaeology Concentration, Biological Anthropology Concentration, Cultural and Linguistic Anthropology Concentration, Medical Anthropology and Global Health Concentration
Description: The Anthropology major introduces students to the comparative study of human diversity and the critical analysis of the concept of "culture." The discipline is conventionally divided into four sub-fields: cultural anthropology, linguistic anthropology, biological anthropology, and archaeology. At Penn, we offer courses in all four sub-fields as well as in medical anthropology. Students may choose to concentrate in any one of the following four areas: Archaeology, Biological Anthropology, Cultural and Linguistic Anthropology, or Medical Anthropology and Global Health.

Concentration: Design Concentration, Intensive Major
Description: The undergraduate major in architecture is a liberal arts degree in the College of Arts and Sciences. The major gives students a deep and broad understanding of architecture as a cultural practice. Students learn about architecture’s history, theories and technologies in the context of global cultures. They also become proficient in the skills needed to represent architectural ideas, including drawing, modeling, and digital software. With its strong and diverse curriculum, the major prepares students for graduate studies in architecture and its allied disciplines of landscape architecture, urban planning and historic preservation. It also provides a strong foundation for students who want to pursue careers in a wide range of fields from law and business to engineering, public policy and the visual arts.

Requirements: Application requirements are for admission to the undergraduate school (College of Arts and Sciences) rather than directly to the major. Key components include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Powered by Scoir; Penn-specific Application Essay; Official High School Transcript; School Report; Letters of Recommendation (1 from a counselor and 2 from teachers); Mid-Year Report; and the Final Report for enrolling students. Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT) are optional for the 2024-25 application cycle.
Description: Biochemistry is the study of the chemistry of life. It provides the foundation for the revolutionary developments in biotechnology and genetic engineering that are having a major impact in areas ranging from medicine to forensics to bioremediation. Biochemistry majors study the major classes of biological molecules: proteins, nucleic acids, lipids and carbohydrates. They learn the chemical principles that underlie the function of these molecules in the processes that sustain life. All biochemistry majors do a two-semester research project with a faculty preceptor. The major is appropriate for students interested in careers in the biological and chemical sciences as well as in the health professions. There is a BS and a BA version of the major. The BA degree is designed for students who want a somewhat less intensive science program than the BS biochemistry major, perhaps because they want to combine it with a second major or because they want more elective time for other courses, perhaps in the arts and humanities. The BA degree can also serve as preparation for careers in industry or public service.

The Bachelor of Arts (BA) with a major in Biology is intended for students who are interested in biology but do not plan to attend graduate school in the life sciences or a health professions school. Students in the College of Arts and Sciences may complete a major in Biology for the BA degree. The requirements are distinct from those for the Bachelor of Arts degree with a major in Biology that may be completed by students in the College of Liberal and Professional Studies. Requirements for the major are listed below. In addition, students must complete the General Requirement of the College of Arts and Sciences.

Requirements: To apply for undergraduate admission at the University of Pennsylvania, prospective students must submit the following: The Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, a Counselor Recommendation, and two Teacher Recommendations. A Mid-Year Report is required for all admitted students, and a Final Report is required for all enrolling students. As of the 2024-2025 application cycle, applicants are required to submit either SAT or ACT scores. An interview is optional and offered based on availability. Applicants with a background in fine arts may also submit an optional supplement.
Description: Biophysics is an interdisciplinary field that applies the theories and methods of physics, chemistry, and mathematics to understand how biological systems work. Its scope is vast, covering all scales of biological organization, from the single molecule to the cell, from the organism to the ecosystem. Biophysics has grown very rapidly in recent years, leading to new opportunities for careers at the cutting edge of science. Undergraduates who major in biophysics at Penn can participate fully in this excitement through research. They will acquire a solid foundation in the physical and life sciences that will prepare them for a variety of careers in scientific research, medicine, and the biotechnology industry. The Biophysics Major is appropriate for students who are planning graduate study in biophysics or a related area, such as molecular biology or neuroscience, or the professional schools of medicine, dentistry, or law.

Requirements: Prospective students apply to one of Penn’s four undergraduate schools, not to a specific major. The application requirements are for admission to the university's undergraduate program. The required components include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Essays, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report, Final Report (for admitted students), and an application fee or fee waiver.
Description: The Department of Chemistry offers several majors to accommodate student interests. The Bachelor of Arts (BA) major is less intensive than the Bachelor of Science (BS) majors and is designed for those students who desire a strong background in chemistry but who do not intend to pursue graduate school in chemistry. The BA in chemistry is also an excellent option for those who have a double major. In addition to chemistry majors, we also offer submatriculation programs for master’s degrees in chemistry and in education, as well as a minor in chemistry.

Requirements: To apply as a first-year student, applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Essay, an official High School Transcript, a School Report, a Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, a Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report upon enrollment.
Description: The undergraduate program in Cinema and Media Studies provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the history, theory, and aesthetics of moving images. Students learn to analyze film, television, and new media in a variety of contexts, considering their formal properties as well as their relationship to culture, society, and technology. The major emphasizes critical thinking, close analysis, and strong writing skills. Courses cover a wide range of topics, including silent cinema, Hollywood genres, international film movements, documentary, animation, television studies, and digital media. Students have the opportunity to explore filmmaking through production courses and to gain practical experience through internships. The program prepares students for careers in the film and media industries, as well as for graduate study in related fields.

Requirements: To apply, prospective students must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application must include Penn-specific essays, an official high school transcript, a school report, three letters of recommendation (one from a counselor and two from teachers), a Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report upon completion of the academic year. An application fee or fee waiver is also required. Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT) are optional for the 2024-25 admissions cycle.
Concentration: Classical Languages and Literature, Classical Civilization, Ancient History, Mediterranean Archaeology
Description: The Classical Studies major offers a multi-disciplinary approach to the study of the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, allowing students to explore the interconnected cultures of the ancient Mediterranean. Students in the Classical Studies major can take courses in the art, archaeology, history, literature, and philosophy of the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, and can also study the ancient Greek and Latin languages. Because of the multi-disciplinary nature of the major, students who major in Classical Studies will learn how to synthesize a wide variety of evidence (textual, material, visual, etc.) and thus prepare themselves for a wide range of future careers.

Concentration: Language; Mind, Brain and Behavior; Cognitive Neuroscience; Computation and Cognition; Psychology: Mind, Brain and Behavior; Language and the Mind
Description: Cognitive Science is the study of the mind and its processes. It is an interdisciplinary field, combining results and insights from psychology, computer science, linguistics, philosophy, and neuroscience. Work in cognitive science has had a major impact on our understanding of language, perception, action, memory, reasoning, decision making, emotion, and consciousness; it has also led to the design of intelligent systems that can perform complex tasks that formerly required human intelligence.

Requirements: Application requirements are for admission into the undergraduate school (College of Arts and Sciences), not the specific major. Applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. Required materials include Penn-specific essays, an official high school transcript, a school report, three letters of recommendation (one from a counselor and two from teachers), and a Mid-Year Report. Admitted students must submit a Final Report. For the application cycle for Fall 2025 entry and beyond, applicants are expected to submit ACT or SAT scores.
Concentration: Communication and Public Service (ComPS), Communication, Culture, and Media, Political Communication, Data and Network Science, Critical Journalism
Description: The undergraduate program in Communication is rooted in the liberal arts tradition, providing a broad understanding of the role of communication in society, and a critical framework for analyzing communication institutions, processes, and effects. The curriculum is designed to help students think systematically about communication and to express those thoughts clearly. Courses in the major examine communication from a variety of theoretical and methodological perspectives. They offer students the knowledge and analytical skills to understand and evaluate communication theories and research. Communication majors have the option of selecting a concentration within the major.

Requirements: Application requirements are for general first-year admission to the University of Pennsylvania's undergraduate schools, as students declare their major after matriculating. The application checklist includes: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific essays, official high school transcript, school report, counselor recommendation, two teacher recommendations, mid-year report, final report, and an application fee or fee waiver. For the 2024-25 application cycle, submission of SAT or ACT scores is optional.
Description: The major in Comparative Literature allows students to bring together their passion for the literatures and cultures of different parts of the world. As a discipline, Comparative Literature is founded on the belief that literary texts can only be fully understood in a comparative framework. This means that at Penn, students not only take courses in a variety of literary traditions, they also learn how to think comparatively about what they read. The major has two main components: coursework in Comparative Literature and coursework in two foreign literature departments. In their Comparative Literature courses, students learn how to analyze and compare texts from a variety of theoretical, historical, and generic perspectives. In their foreign literature courses, students develop the in-depth knowledge of individual literary traditions and languages that all true comparative work requires. The flexibility of the major allows students to shape their own program of study in consultation with the undergraduate chair.

Requirements: Prospective students apply to one of Penn’s four undergraduate schools, in this case, the College of Arts & Sciences. The application requirements are managed by the central undergraduate admissions office. The required application materials include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, Two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report, Final Report, and a $75 application fee or fee waiver. For students applying through the Early Decision program, the Early Decision Agreement is also required.
Description: The Criminology major is an interdisciplinary program that focuses on the problem of crime and the criminal justice system. The curriculum draws on a wide variety of disciplines, including Criminology, Sociology, History, Law, and Political Science. The major is designed for students interested in studying the causes and consequences of crime, the structure and function of the criminal justice system, and the social, cultural, and political contexts of law and justice. The major provides a strong foundation for students interested in careers in law, criminal justice, public policy, and social service, as well as for graduate study in Criminology, Sociology, or Law.

Requirements:
The following is a list of all the required application materials for first-year applicants:

- Common Application or Coalition Application, Powered by Scoir
- Penn-specific Application Essay
- Official high school transcript
- School Report
- Counselor Recommendation
- Two Teacher Recommendations
- Mid-Year Report
- Final Report
- Standardized test scores (optional for 2024-25 admissions cycle)
- $75 application fee or fee waiver
Concentration: Art, Technology, and the Future; City and Social Change; Communication, Information, and Media; Mind and Materiality
Description: The undergraduate major in Design leads to a BA degree in the College of Arts and Sciences. The major combines hands-on-making with a critical and historical framing of design. The major emphasizes critical thinking and creative production and offers a curriculum that is both broad and deep, allowing students flexibility to follow their own interests and develop a unique course of study. The major requires 13 courses: five core courses in design and four courses in a specific concentration that builds on the foundations of the core. Two studio courses and two seminar/lecture courses in a concentration provide students with depth and a critical framework for understanding their work. Two additional electives, from any concentration, and two major-related courses, complete the major. Students take a final thesis course in the fall of their senior year. This course prepares them for a capstone project that is presented to the public in a final exhibition at the end of the spring semester.

Requirements: Application requirements are not specified for the major directly. Students apply to one of Penn's undergraduate schools, in this case, the College of Arts & Sciences. The general first-year application requirements include: Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Application Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Academic Teacher Recommendations, a Mid-Year Report, and an application fee or fee waiver. Standardized test scores are optional.
Description: The major in Earth Science focuses on the Earth as a complex system, and includes a solid foundation in the core disciplines of geology, biology,chemistry, and physics. The Bachelor of Arts (BA) in Earth and Environmental Science is intended for students who wish to pursue a career or graduate work in environmental policy, environmental law, management, journalism, or education. It provides a broad background in Earth and Environmental Science, and some flexibility in the selection of upper-level courses.

ProgramName: East Asian Languages and Civilizations, BA
Requirements: All prospective students apply to the University of Pennsylvania using the Common Application or Coalition Application. The application must include: an official high school transcript, a school report, letters of recommendation (one from a counselor and two from teachers), and a mid-year report. If applying through Early Decision, an Early Decision Agreement is also required. A final report is required for all matriculating students.
Concentration: China, Japan
Description: The major in East Asian Languages and Civilizations (EALC) provides students with a broad and deep understanding of the cultures of East Asia (China, Japan, and Korea). The curriculum is designed to provide students with the linguistic competency, disciplinary methodology, and factual knowledge to pursue a professional career or graduate studies in a field related to East Asia. The program has three key components: language training, broad foundational coursework in the humanities and social sciences, and a specialization in one area of East Asian studies. In consultation with the undergraduate chair, students build a program of study that is at once comprehensive and tailored to their own intellectual interests. The language component requires four years of Chinese, Japanese, or Korean. The foundational coursework gives students a broad overview of the history, literature, and cultures of East Asia. The specialization gives students the opportunity to bring their linguistic and disciplinary training to bear on one particular area of interest. In order to achieve the goals of the major, students are required to take a minimum of sixteen courses: eight in language and eight in non-language content courses. These requirements are described in more detail below. Students are encouraged to take advantage of Penn’s many study abroad programs, as well as the full range of courses in EALC and related departments and programs.

Concentration: Advanced Theory Concentration, Data Analytics Concentration, Finance Concentration, International Economics Concentration, Public Policy Concentration, Behavioral Economics Concentration, Strategic Management Concentration, Individualized Concentration
Description: The undergraduate economics major is designed to provide students with a firm grounding in modern economic theory, statistical and econometric methods, and their applications. It is designed to be flexible, allowing students to construct a program of study that suits their interests and goals. Students in the major may go on to graduate school in economics, law, medicine, or business; others take jobs in government, private firms, or the non-profit sector. An important part of the economics major is the senior research requirement, in which students have an opportunity to engage in economic research under the supervision of a faculty member.

Requirements: First-year applicants to the University of Pennsylvania must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application, which includes a Penn-specific Essay. Required documents include an Official High School Transcript, a School Report, one Counselor Recommendation, and two Teacher Recommendations. Applicants must also submit a Mid-Year Report. A Final Report is required for all students who enroll.
Concentration: American Literature and Culture, British and Other Anglophone Literature, Cinema and Media Studies, Creative Writing, Generalist, Genre and Poetics, Global and Transnational English, Literature and Culture before the 17th Century, Literature and Culture from the 17th Century to the Present, Theoretical and Cross-Cultural Studies
Description: The English major at Penn offers an opportunity to study a rich variety of literary, cultural, and historical documents, from ancient epics to contemporary films. Our department includes many distinguished scholars who are also dedicated teachers. Our courses are typically small and stress active student participation. Students are encouraged to develop their own interests and to work closely with faculty members in directed readings and honors projects. The major itself combines a focus on traditional historical fields with a wide range of theoretical and interdisciplinary pursuits. It has long enjoyed an international reputation in areas such as Renaissance literature, American literature, modernism, and contemporary poetry. It has also emerged as a vital center for the study of ethnic literature, gender and sexuality studies, cultural studies, and critical theory. The English major helps students to become perceptive readers, critical thinkers, and strong writers—skills that provide a foundation for careers in a wide range of professions, including law, business, publishing, journalism, education, and the arts.

Concentration: ['Environmental Biology', 'Environmental Policy', 'Earth Science', 'Sustainability and Environmental Management', 'Environmental Humanities', 'Global Environmental Systems', 'Individualized Concentration']
Description: The Environmental Studies major provides students with the intellectual and practical tools to understand and address pressing environmental challenges. The major attracts a diverse group of students who are curious about the many intersections between human societies and the biophysical environment, and prepares them to pursue careers in a wide array of fields. The interdisciplinary nature of the major enables students to integrate knowledge from across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, and our emphasis on experiential learning—including field courses, undergraduate research, study abroad, internships, and civic engagement—gives students hands-on opportunities to apply their knowledge. Students in the major select one of seven concentrations, each of which has a distinct curriculum and area of focus. We also offer a General major option for students with an interest in Environmental Studies but whose academic interests do not fit well with any of the defined concentrations. All Environmental Studies majors take an introductory course (ENVS 1000), a statistics course, and a senior seminar in which they complete an independent research project that integrates their coursework with their concentration. For College students, the Environmental Studies major fulfills the Natural Science & Math requirement of the Sector Requirement.

Requirements: General application requirements for first-year applicants include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report (due after first-marking period grades are available), and a Final Report for admitted students who choose to enroll. An application fee or fee waiver is also required. For applicants to the College of Arts & Sciences with an interest in Fine Arts, an optional portfolio of artwork may be submitted as a supplement to the application.
Description: The undergraduate major in Fine Arts is intended for students who wish to pursue a rigorous liberal arts education and a studio-based visual arts curriculum. Students may work in a variety of disciplines, including animation and 3D modeling, drawing, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, and video. Through a combination of core studios, art history courses, and a wide array of studio electives, the curriculum provides an open intellectual framework that allows for a deep and broad-based investigation into the practice of making art today.

ProgramName: Francophone, Italian and Germanic Studies, BA
Description: The major in Francophone, Italian and Germanic Studies (FIGS) allows students to study the cultures of the French-, Italian- and German-speaking worlds from a comparative and interdisciplinary perspective. This major is ideal for students with an interest in two of these three areas. A major that combines two of the three subjects allows students to develop an intercultural perspective that enhances their understanding of both fields. The FIGS major consists of twelve courses, six in a primary language and culture and four in a secondary language and culture, plus two additional electives that can come from either area. In consultation with the FIGS advisor, each student will design a course of study that reflects their interests in the language, literature, history and culture of the Francophone, Italian and German-speaking worlds. Courses are taught in English and in the target languages. FIGS majors who wish to study abroad are encouraged to do so and can count courses taken abroad toward their major requirements.

Concentration: Feminist Studies, Global Gender and Sexuality Studies, Health and Disability, Individualized Concentration
Description: The undergraduate program in Gender, Sexuality, and Women’s Studies (GSWS) offers students the opportunity to pursue interdisciplinary study in a variety of fields concerned with gender, sexuality, and women. Students learn to think critically about the social construction of gender and the ways in which gender and sexuality have been defined and have operated in various historical and cultural contexts. The major is broadly interdisciplinary and requires students to take courses in the humanities, social sciences, and policy-oriented fields. The GSWS major is flexible, with a required core of introductory, theory, and research courses and many options for electives in several areas of concentration.

Concentration: Bioethics and Society, Disease and Society, Gender, Sexuality and Health, Global Health, Health Care Markets and Finance, Health Policy and Law, Race, Ethnicity and Health
Description: The Health and Societies (HSOC) major provides students with a multi-disciplinary framework for understanding the social, cultural, political, economic, and ethical dimensions of health, illness, and medical care in human societies, past and present. The curriculum is designed to help students think critically about the complex relationships that link health to social and cultural contexts. All students majoring in Health & Societies choose a concentration within the major. Concentrations enable students to acquire a deeper understanding of a specific facet of the major and to hone their analytical skills by working closely with a faculty member in their area of interest. Concentrations consist of four courses. Students also complete a capstone course in their senior year.
ScholarshipType: Need-based (including Penn Grant, Federal Pell Grant, FSEOG, State Grants)

Concentration: Portuguese and Brazilian Studies
Description: The major in Hispanic Studies offers a broad and comprehensive curriculum in the literatures and cultures of the Spanish-speaking world: Spain, Latin America and the U.S. Courses are taught in Spanish. The curriculum combines broad survey courses with more specialized courses on specific topics, periods, authors and genres. Students are required to develop a comprehensive knowledge of Hispanic literatures and cultures from the Middle Ages to the present, as well as the analytical skills to engage critically with primary and secondary texts. Students majoring in Hispanic Studies also have the option of declaring a concentration in Portuguese and Brazilian Studies, which provides a more specialized curricular path including two required courses and several electives.

Requirements: First-year applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Essay, an official high school transcript, a school report, one counselor recommendation, two teacher recommendations, a Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report. An interview is optional.
Concentration: Architecture Concentration, General History of Art Concentration, Museums, Markets and Collecting Concentration, History of Art Honors Program with Thesis
Description: The History of Art major is intended to provide students with a broad and deep understanding of the history of art and architecture of a variety of periods and geographical areas, and to equip them with the tools of visual and historical analysis necessary to make a contribution to the field. Majors are encouraged to pursue an interdisciplinary and global course of study and to take advantage of the rich offerings across the university as they craft a personalized program of courses that will culminate in a capstone seminar. The capstone seminar is an intensive research and writing course designed to familiarize students with the most advanced methods in the discipline and to produce a substantial research paper. For students considering graduate work in the field, for those interested in museum or gallery work, and for those who simply wish to explore a particular area of art history in depth, the department offers a variety of specialized concentrations, as well as an honors program that provides an in-depth and challenging course of study.

Requirements: Prospective students apply to one of Penn’s four undergraduate schools, not to a specific major. The general application requirements for first-year applicants include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Essays, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report, and Final Report. Standardized test scores (SAT or ACT) are also required.
Description: The History Major is designed to stimulate and gratify students' curiosity about the past, to sharpen their critical and analytical skills, and to provide them with intellectual perspectives that will be of great value whatever their future pursuits. Students have maximum freedom in the choice of their courses, but the Major's requirements are meant to ensure that their choices are both coherent and broad. We especially want our students to think about the nature of history itself. The Proseminar, the Research Seminar and the optional Honors Thesis all emphasize historiographical issues as well as research methods.

The Individualized Major allows students to combine courses from several departments and programs into a coherent field of study not represented in any of the College’s established majors. The major is interdepartmental and interdisciplinary in nature. A student must have a cumulative GPA of 3.0 or above to apply for an Individualized Major. Students interested in this major should meet with a College advisor to discuss their ideas and to begin to search for a faculty advisor. The application to the major should be submitted by the end of sophomore year.

Requirements:
Prospective students apply to the University of Pennsylvania's undergraduate program, not to the specific major. The general application requirements include:
- Common Application or Coalition Application
- Penn-specific Essay
- Official High School Transcript
- School Report
- Counselor Recommendation
- Two Teacher Recommendations
- Mid-Year Report
- Standardized test scores (SAT or ACT) are optional for the 2024-25 admissions cycle.
Concentration: Commercial & Legal Institutions of the World Economy Track, Conflict & Security Track, Foreign Policy & Diplomacy Track, Global Governance & International Organizations Track, Global Health & Environment Track, International Political Economy & Development Track, Latin American & Caribbean Studies Track, Middle Eastern & North African Studies Track, Russian & East European Studies Track, South Asian Studies Track, Sub-Saharan African Studies Track, United States in the World Track, Western European Studies Track
Description: The International Relations (IR) Program at Penn is an interdisciplinary major in the College of Arts and Sciences that is jointly administered by the Political Science Department and the Lauder Institute. We offer an undergraduate education in world politics that is balanced, comprehensive, and rigorous. Students investigate the political, economic, and cultural interactions of a wide range of state and non-state actors at the local, national, and international levels. Students become familiar with the historical evolution of the international system and its current-day workings while engaging questions of ethics, justice, and the distribution of power. The IR major requires that students demonstrate a proficiency in a foreign language and complete a study abroad experience. In addition, we encourage our students to seek out internships that will help them gain first-hand experience in a variety of international fields and professions.

Concentration: ['Africa', 'Asia', 'Europe', 'Latin America']
Description: The International Studies Major (ISMA) is a joint major with the Wharton School that provides students with the opportunity to combine a business education with a liberal arts focus on international studies. Students complete the full Wharton curriculum as well as 14-course units in the College of Arts & Sciences. These courses include language proficiency as well as area studies and international relations coursework. The major allows students to choose a concentration in a particular geographic region of the world: Africa, Asia, Europe, or Latin America. This joint major is only open to students admitted to the Huntsman Program.

Requirements: Application requirements are not specific to the Jewish Studies, BA major but are for general undergraduate admission to the College of Arts and Sciences. Requirements include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, three Letters of Recommendation, a Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report upon matriculation. Standardized test scores (SAT or ACT) are also required.
Description: The Jewish Studies Program at the University of Pennsylvania provides a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary approach to Jewish civilization from antiquity to the present. As an academic field, Jewish studies is anchored in the traditional humanities—in the mastery of languages and the close reading of texts from a wide variety of genres—but it has also come to embrace the full gamut of approaches of the social sciences. The Jewish studies major will provide the basic tools for all students to pursue this inter-disciplinary field while encouraging each to develop his or her specific interests. This major can be an excellent preparation for careers in Jewish education, the rabbinate, Jewish communal service, and graduate work in Jewish studies. For students whose main interests lie elsewhere, a major in Jewish Studies will also constitute a superb liberal arts education and an unusually rich opportunity to explore questions of history, literature, religion, and culture that have broad applicability to other fields.

Requirements: First-year applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application, including the Penn Writing Supplement. Required supporting documents include an official high school transcript, a School Report, one counselor recommendation, and two teacher recommendations. A Mid-Year Report must be submitted when first-term/second-quarter senior grades are available, and a Final Report is required for all matriculating students. An interview is optional and not guaranteed.
Description: The Latin American and Latinx Studies (LALS) Program offers an interdisciplinary major and minor to students in the College of Arts and Sciences. LALS offers students the opportunity to learn about the diverse histories, politics, economies, and cultures of the region as well as those of its peoples in the U.S. By combining courses offered in several departments, LALS introduces students to the study of Latin America and the Caribbean, while also providing them with the opportunity to specialize in one or two disciplines and/or one or two areas of the region. A certificate in LALS is available for Wharton undergraduates, and a minor for undergraduates in the Schools of Engineering and Applied Science and Nursing. Penn undergraduates in all four schools can get a language certificate in Portuguese, Quechua or Spanish.

Requirements: First-year applicants apply for admission to one of Penn’s four undergraduate schools, not to a specific major. The Law and Society major is in the College of Arts and Sciences. General application requirements include: Common Application or Coalition Application, Powered by Scoir; Penn-specific Essay; Official High School Transcript; School Report; Counselor Recommendation; Two Teacher Recommendations; Mid-Year Report; and a Final Report for admitted students who enroll.
Concentration: Law and Social Structure, Law and Social Change, Global and Comparative Law
Description: The Law and Society major provides an interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary liberal arts approach to the study of law and legal institutions, and their impact on society. In this major, law is studied as a social institution, in the context of both the humanities and the social sciences. Students are encouraged to develop a critical understanding of legal institutions, and of law in its social, cultural, and historical contexts. Law and Society majors take a core set of courses offered by the Sociology Department, and then select courses from Sociology and from several other departments in the College of Arts and Sciences, and from the Wharton School. Students are introduced to the various modes of inquiry used in legal studies, including historical, philosophical, and social science approaches.

Requirements: Application requirements are for admission to the undergraduate College of Arts & Sciences. Required documents include the Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Essay, an official high school transcript, a school report, one counselor recommendation, two teacher recommendations, a mid-year report, and a final report. An application fee or fee waiver is also required. Standardized tests like the SAT or ACT are optional for the 2024-25 application cycle.
Concentration: ['Concentration in American Sign Language and Deaf Studies (ASLD)', 'General Linguistics Concentration', 'Concentration in Language and Cognition', 'Concentration in Language and Social Structure', 'Concentration in Language and the Brain']
Description: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language. It is a multifaceted discipline that addresses the structure of language (phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics) as well as the social and cultural aspects of language (sociolinguistics, historical linguistics), how language is acquired (language acquisition), and how it is represented in the mind (psycholinguistics, neurolinguistics). A major in linguistics offers an excellent basis for a variety of careers in fields such as education, computer science, psychology, law, and many other fields.

Requirements: Application requirements are not specific to the Logic, Information, & Computation major but are for admission to the undergraduate school (the College of Arts and Sciences). First-year applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. Required components include the Penn-specific Essay, an official high school transcript, a School Report, a mid-year report, a final report, and three letters of recommendation (one from a counselor and two from teachers).
Concentration: ['Cognitive Science (LGIC-COGS)', 'Computation and Logic (LGIC-COMP)', 'Logic and Language (LGIC-LANG)', 'Mathematical Logic (LGIC-MATH)']
Description: The Logic, Information, and Computation (LGIC) major, administered by the Department of Mathematics, is an interdisciplinary major that provides students with a strong foundation in the core principles of logic, computation, and information, especially as they are applied in mathematics, computer science, linguistics, and philosophy. The LGIC major is designed to appeal to students with a variety of interests, since the major allows students to choose one of four concentrations: Cognitive Science (LGIC-COGS), Computation and Logic (LGIC-COMP), Logic and Language (LGIC-LANG), and Mathematical Logic (LGIC-MATH).

The Mathematical Economics major is an interdepartmental major between the Economics Department (in the School of Arts and Sciences) and the Statistics and Data Science Department (in the Wharton School). The major is very challenging and is suitable only for those students with a strong interest in and an aptitude for mathematics. The major seeks to endow the student with the basic tools of the professional economist. It provides an excellent background for graduate study in economics. Mathematical Economics is a major in the College of Arts and Sciences. It does not lead to a degree from the Wharton School.

Requirements: Prospective students must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. Required application components include the Penn-specific Essay, an Official High School Transcript, a School Report, one Counselor Recommendation, and two Teacher Recommendations. A Mid-Year Report is required when first-term senior grades are available, and a Final Report is required for admitted students who choose to enroll. Standardized test scores (ACT or SAT) are optional for the 2024-25 admissions cycle.
Concentration: ['Applied Mathematics and Computational Science Concentration', 'Mathematical Biology Concentration']
Description: The major in Mathematics is intended for students who are interested in mathematics and its applications. It is also for those who plan to pursue graduate work in mathematics, or in such related fields as statistics, operations research, computer science, economics, finance, or business. For those interested primarily in applications or in the teaching of mathematics, it is possible to specialize in those areas. Flexibility is the keynote of the mathematics major. Please see the Mathematics Department website for more information.

Requirements: Prospective students apply to the University of Pennsylvania's undergraduate program, typically through the College of Arts & Sciences, and declare their major after matriculating. The application requirements are for general first-year admission and include: Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report (due after first-term senior year grades are available), and Final Report (for admitted students who choose to enroll). Standardized testing (SAT/ACT) is optional for the 2024-25 application cycle.
Description: The major in Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures is designed for students who seek a linguistically-grounded and interdisciplinary approach to the study of the Middle East. The major builds upon the language and culture foundation of the area of the student's primary language of study. Students will choose one of the five languages taught in the department as a focus language: Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi/Urdu, Persian, or Turkish. Students will take two advanced language courses beyond the language requirement, and a total of ten courses that count toward the major. Majors are required to take NELC 0100 Introduction to the Middle East, as well as a senior research seminar, NELC 3000, in which they will produce a capstone research paper. The remaining six courses will consist of departmentally-approved courses, three of which must be at the 2000-level or higher.

Requirements: Prospective undergraduate students apply to a specific undergraduate school at the University of Pennsylvania, not to a major. The application is submitted via the Common Application or Coalition Application. General requirements include: the application form, a Penn-specific essay, official high school transcript, a school report, letters of recommendation (from a counselor and two teachers), a mid-year report, and a final report for matriculating students. There are no specific requirements listed for admission directly into the Modern Middle Eastern Studies major.
Concentration: Anthropology and Sociology of the Middle East, History of the Middle East, Islamic Studies, Politics of the Middle East
Description: The major in Modern Middle Eastern Studies (MMES) offers a course of study for students interested in the politics, history, religion, languages, and cultures of the region. This interdisciplinary major provides an opportunity for students to study the Middle East using the methodologies of various departments, including Anthropology, History, History of Art, Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Political Science, and Religious Studies. Majors receive thorough grounding in the history and politics of the modern Middle East, gain proficiency in a Middle Eastern language, and take a sequence of courses organized around one of four distinct concentrations: Anthropology and Sociology, History, Islamic Studies, and Politics. The major is designed to provide a sound liberal arts background for students interested in pursuing graduate studies or in careers in which a knowledge of the Middle East is essential, such as diplomacy, government, journalism, and business.

Concentration: ['Musicology', 'Ethnomusicology', 'Theory', 'Composition', 'Performance', 'Jazz and Popular Music', 'Music Technology']
Description: The Music major at Penn is designed to allow students to explore music from a variety of perspectives. The curriculum develops students' musicianship skills while offering a background in a variety of musical traditions and repertoires. Students majoring in music explore the cultural and historical contexts of music, as well as the theoretical and compositional techniques that underlie musical works. Music majors gain a strong background in music while also receiving a broad liberal arts education. This prepares them for graduate study in music, as well as for careers in many fields, including arts administration, business, education, law, medicine, music criticism and journalism, and performance, as well as other related areas.

Neuroscience is an interdisciplinary major that provides a strong background for students interested in the biological bases of thought and behavior. The curriculum is intended for students who wish to pursue graduate work in neuroscience, medicine, or related fields, and to provide the appropriate science background for other professions such as law, business, and education. Required courses are drawn from biology, chemistry, mathematics, physics, and psychology.

Nutrition science is the study of how food affects the body. It covers a wide range of topics, from the biochemical processes involved in metabolism to the social and behavioral factors that influence food choices. The Nutrition Science major at Penn is a basic science-based curriculum that prepares students for careers in medicine and other health professions, biomedical research, and public health. All students in the Nutrition Science major must complete the pre-med requirements. Our graduates are competitive candidates for medical, dental, and other health professional schools. Graduates of the program are also well prepared for graduate study leading to research, and for positions in industry, government, and other institutions that require a strong science background. All students in the Nutrition Science major take courses in chemistry, biology, physics, and math to establish a solid foundation in the basic sciences. Students in the major also take a sequence of three nutrition courses, including NUTR 1000 Nutrition and the Consumer, NUTR 2000 Nutrition and Metabolism, and NUTR 3300 Nutrition and the Life Cycle. Through these courses, students will gain an understanding of the functions of nutrients, the metabolic and physiologic consequences of nutrient deficiencies and excesses in human populations, and the role of nutrition in health and disease.

Requirements: The following is a list of items you’ll need to complete your application: Common Application or Coalition Application, Powered by Scoir; Penn-specific Essay; $75 application fee or fee waiver; Official high school transcript; School Report; Counselor Recommendation; Two Teacher Recommendations; Mid-Year Report (due when first-term senior grades are available); Final Report (due for matriculating students only).
Concentration: Philosophy and Science (PASC)
Description: The major in philosophy is designed to acquaint students with the fundamentals of philosophical reasoning and to provide them with a sophisticated understanding of the major figures and periods in the history of philosophy, as well as the central problems and areas of the discipline in the present day. Through their coursework, students will develop and hone their abilities to think and write with clarity, rigor, and intellectual imagination. The Department encourages its majors to pursue a broad liberal arts education, and many of our students double-major in a variety of other fields. For those who choose to continue their philosophical studies in graduate school, we offer a rich and demanding curriculum; however, the philosophy major also provides an excellent preparation for many other professions, including law, medicine, business, and public service.

Concentration: Choice, Behavior and Markets, Constitutionalism and Governance, Distributive Justice, Globalization, Public Policy and a Fourth Course
Description: The Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) major has a long and distinguished history. It was born at Oxford University in the 1920s out of the conviction that study of the great modern works of social, political, and economic thought would be a good preparation for students entering the civil service and public life. It has since become a highly successful and influential program of study around the world. The PPE major at Penn provides a multidisciplinary education to students who want to become leaders in public affairs and in the national and international business communities. The major rests on the view that an understanding of the contemporary world requires knowledge of the principles of economic and political science, informed by the rigor of philosophical thought.

Requirements: To apply for first-year admission to the University of Pennsylvania, applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, which includes a personal essay, along with a Penn-specific Essay. Additional required documents include a $75 application fee or fee waiver, official high school transcript, School Report, a Counselor Recommendation, and two Teacher Recommendations. Applicants must also submit a Mid-Year Report and a Final Report upon availability. For the 2024-25 admissions cycle, applicants are required to submit either SAT or ACT scores.
Description: The Physics B.A. is a more flexible program for students who may be interested in a career in medicine, law, business, education, or other fields. Although the B.A. degree may be sufficient to qualify students for some positions in industry or government, it is not usually considered adequate preparation for doctoral study in physics. It can, however, provide an excellent background for graduate work in other sciences.

Requirements: To apply as a first-year student, applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application includes a personal essay and a Penn-specific essay. Required supporting documents include an official high school transcript, a school report, one counselor recommendation, and two teacher recommendations. A Mid-Year Report with first semester/trimester senior grades is also required. Standardized test scores (SAT or ACT) are optional. An alumni interview is also part of the application process.
Concentration: ['American Politics (AP)', 'Comparative Politics (CP)', 'International Relations (IR)', 'Political Theory (PT)', 'Public Policy and Governance (PPG)', 'Race, Ethnicity and Politics (REP)']
Description: The Undergraduate Program in Political Science is one of the largest undergraduate majors in the School of Arts and Sciences. It is also one of the most distinguished. Its faculty have international reputations, are leaders in their respective fields, and have been recognized both by the American Political Science Association and the University of Pennsylvania for their distinguished research and their teaching excellence. Our goal is to provide students with a deep and comprehensive understanding of politics. Politics is the process through which societies make collective decisions and determine how to distribute power and resources. The study of politics at Penn therefore encompasses a very broad range of topics, including: the meaning of democracy, the nature of personal liberty, the causes of war and peace, the sources of political and economic development, the challenges of environmental protection, the role of international organizations, the determinants of election outcomes, the nature of public opinion, and the meaning of justice and equality. To address these and other important questions, we offer an array of courses organized around four broad subfields of Political Science: American Politics, Comparative Politics, International Relations, and Political Theory.

Concentration: Cognitive Neuroscience, Clinical & Positive Psychology, Social & Personality Psychology
Description: Psychology is a science devoted to understanding human behavior, and the major at Penn is designed to give students an understanding of the important questions, methodologies, and findings in the major areas of this diverse field. Core course requirements ensure that students are exposed to the social, cognitive, developmental, and biological bases of behavior, and develop skills in the research methods and statistical techniques that are used to advance our understanding of these topics. Advanced coursework allows students to explore areas of personal interest in greater depth. Students are also encouraged to get involved in the research of the department by taking independent study courses with faculty members, or through paid research assistantships.

Requirements: Application requirements are for undergraduate admission to the College of Arts and Sciences, not specifically for the Religious Studies major. General requirements include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Supplement, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, Two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report upon matriculation.
Description: What is religion? How can we best study it? The major and minor in Religious Studies provide students with the opportunity to explore the variety of religious traditions, and to learn different methods and approaches to understanding them. The Religious Studies curriculum reflects a wide spectrum of historical and cultural traditions, ranging from the ancient Near East to modern America, from the Abrahamic faiths of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam to the religions of Asia and Africa. The curriculum also introduces majors and minors to a variety of theories and methods to study those religious traditions. In the major, each student works with a faculty advisor to develop a course of study that reflects the student's own particular interests, while also meeting the requirements of the major. The major thus offers a well-defined structure, but also considerable flexibility. As they take a range of courses in the department, students become acquainted with religious phenomena and learn about various scholarly approaches to the academic study of religion (e.g., historical, anthropological, sociological, philosophical, literary, etc.). Religious Studies majors and minors develop the ability to read analytically, think critically, and write cogently. They also gain the specific skills to apply these abilities to the cross-cultural study of religion in its historical context, as well as the contemporary role of religion in global affairs.

ProgramName: Russian and East European Studies, BA
Concentration: Russian Language, Literature, and Culture; Russian and East European Studies
Description: The major in Russian and East European Studies offers a choice of two concentrations: Russian Language, Literature, and Culture; and Russian and East European Studies. The major in REES is designed to provide B.A. candidates with a broad, interdisciplinary background in the languages, literatures, cultures, and histories of Russia and Eastern Europe, and a more specific focus for those who intend to go on to an M.A. or Ph.D. program in these fields. Students who complete the major requirements will acquire significant reading and speaking ability in one or two of the region's languages; a sophisticated understanding of the historical, cultural, and social forces that have shaped Russia and Eastern Europe; and the research, analytical, and writing skills that are necessary for advanced work in the humanities and social sciences. Students are strongly encouraged to study abroad in Russia or Eastern Europe for at least one semester or a summer. The Russian and East European Studies Program is an undergraduate component of the Department of Russian and East European Studies. The department's program in Russian and East European Studies is recognized as a National Resource Center by the US Department of Education.

Science, Technology, and Society (STSC) is a liberal arts major that focuses on one of the most important forces in modern life. The major prepares students to understand and participate in a world that is profoundly shaped by science and technology. It provides a strong foundation for citizenship, for careers in law, business, and public policy, as well as for graduate study in the humanities and social sciences. STSC courses analyze the historical, social, political, economic, and cultural dimensions of science, technology, and medicine. Some courses focus on the development of particular sciences or technologies, while others examine specific ethical or policy issues, such as those related to the internet, to health care, or to the environment. All students in the major learn how different disciplines in the humanities and social sciences study science and technology.

Requirements: First-year applicants must submit either the Common Application or Coalition Application. Required documents include: a Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, a Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report. For Early Decision applicants, an Early Decision Agreement is also required.
Concentration: Cities, Communities, and Regions; Global, Transnational, and Comparative Sociology; Law and Society; Quantitative Methods; Sociology of Culture
Description: Sociology is the study of the social lives of people, groups, and societies. It addresses the most challenging issues of our time, from the social causes and consequences of racism, poverty, crime, and environmental degradation to the social dynamics of business, technology, social media, and social movements. Sociology examines how social structures, institutions, and cultures are created and how they affect human action and social change. Sociology provides a unique understanding of how societies function and what can be done to address social problems.

The undergraduate major in South Asia Studies provides an excellent framework for understanding the history, cultures, and societies of this vast, diverse, and important part of the world. South Asia—which encompasses Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka—is home to roughly one-quarter of the world’s population, two of the world’s major religions (Hinduism and Buddhism), one of the world’s largest Muslim populations, and a fascinating array of languages and cultural traditions. The major is broadly interdisciplinary, offering students the opportunity to explore this region from a wide variety of perspectives, including anthropology, archaeology, art history, cinema and media studies, history, history of art, literary and cultural studies, music, political science, religious studies, and sociology. As a part of the major, students are expected to gain proficiency in a South Asian language. The South Asia Studies major prepares students for graduate study as well as a range of professional careers, including education, government, international business, journalism, law, medicine, and non-profit/non-governmental organization (NGO) work.

Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: Performance Concentration, Theatre and Performance Studies Concentration
Description: The Theatre Arts major offers a unique opportunity for students to combine a rigorous, writing-intensive academic course of study with a diverse and challenging artistic practice. The major combines the study of dramatic literature, theatre history, performance theory and criticism, and performance practice within a liberal arts context. Courses embrace a broad spectrum of cross-cultural and interdisciplinary methods, and the faculty brings a wide range of expertise and artistic experience to the program. The major also provides opportunities for students to pursue intensive, pre-professional training in performance, design, and playwriting. Majors participate in an annual season of performances and events through the Theatre Arts Program and Penn Players Student Theatre, and are encouraged to take advantage of the numerous professional theatres located in Philadelphia. Courses in theatre provide credit towards the B.A. degree and are designed to develop students' critical and creative abilities and to expand their understanding of the relationship between theatre and society. Students graduating with a Theatre Arts major have successfully pursued advanced degrees at leading academic and professional training programs, as well as careers in the performing arts, film and television, arts management, casting, dramaturgy, law, education, business, and medicine. The Theatre Arts Program also offers a Minor in Theatre Arts and a Minor in Performance and is a partner in the Music Theatre Minor. Information on all three minors is available on the Theatre Arts website and elsewhere in the Catalog. The Theatre Arts Program is part of a collaborative relationship between the University of Pennsylvania and the Pig Iron Theatre Company, a partnership that supports professional training in devised performance. The Theatre Arts Program also engages in collaborative artistic and academic programming with a number of arts and culture organizations across campus.

Requirements: Application to an undergraduate program like Urban Studies, BA is done through the general first-year application process. The required components are: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific essays, a $75 application fee or fee waiver, official high school transcript, School Report, one counselor recommendation, two teacher recommendations, and a Mid-Year Report. A Final Report is required in June from admitted students who choose to enroll. Standardized tests (SAT/ACT) are optional.
Concentration: Cities and Society; Urban Development and Commerce
Description: The Urban Studies Program at the University of Pennsylvania offers a liberal arts-based, interdisciplinary approach to the study of urban life. The program draws on the social sciences and humanities, as well as the professional schools, to provide students with a broad-based understanding of cities and urban systems. A major in Urban Studies consists of twelve courses. Of these, six are the Urban Studies "core curriculum." The remaining six courses are an area of concentration that the student creates in conjunction with the Urban Studies academic advisor. The Urban Studies major has two concentrations: Cities and Society; and Urban Development and Commerce.

Visual Studies is an interdisciplinary undergraduate major in the College of Arts and Sciences that focuses on vision and visuality in the arts, humanities, and social, and natural sciences. The major consists of a variety of courses that are designed to develop visual literacy and critical seeing.

Requirements: The Africana Studies minor is a six-course program of study. At least four of the courses for the minor must be taken at the University of Pennsylvania. In order to receive credit for the minor, a student must receive a grade of C or better in all courses for the minor. Students interested in the minor should consult the Undergraduate Chair.
Description: The Africana Studies minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to the study of the history, culture and social-political realities of Africans and people of African descent throughout the world. The curriculum seeks to provide students with a deep and broad understanding of the links between the social, economic, political and cultural dimensions of the Africana experience, including the creative expression of these experiences in literature, music, art and dance. The curriculum, therefore, highlights both the historical and contemporary experiences of Africans and their descendants in Africa, the U.S., the Caribbean and Latin America.

Requirements:
The minor in American Public Policy (APPC) requires six courses for a total of six course units.
1. One introductory course on American politics or public policy.
2. One course in statistics.
3. Four elective courses, with at least two at the 2000-level or above.
Concentration: Law and Social Policy, Education Policy, Environmental Policy, Health Policy, Urban Policy and Community Development, Race and Ethnic Policy
Description: The American Public Policy (APPC) minor focuses on the American political process and the analysis of U.S. public policy. It is designed to provide students with the analytic tools necessary for an understanding of the politics and economics of public policy and with in-depth exposure to at least one substantive policy area. Students will develop an understanding of how issues get on the political agenda, how political institutions and processes shape policy choices, and how the consequences of policy are evaluated. They will also gain an understanding of the economic justification for government intervention in the economy, and the potential for government failure. The minor requires a single course in statistics, one introductory course in either microeconomics or American politics, three courses from a list of core courses in public policy analysis and processes, and two courses in a substantive policy area such as education policy, health care policy, environmental policy, or urban policy.

ProgramName: American Sign Language and Deaf Studies Minor
Description: The minor in American Sign Language and Deaf Studies, housed in the Department of Linguistics, consists of six course units. The minor gives students a comprehensive introduction to the language and culture of the Deaf community in the United States. Four courses are in the acquisition of American Sign Language (ASL), and two are in Deaf studies. These two courses are taught in English and have no pre-requisites.

Requirements:
A total of 6 course units are required.

Two courses in Ancient History (ANCH) at any level
Four additional course units chosen from the list below in at least two of the following categories:
Ancient History
Classical Civilization
Greek
Latin
Approved related fields
Description: Ancient history is an interdisciplinary field that draws on literary and material evidence to study the ancient Mediterranean world, from the second millennium BCE to (in some areas) the eighth century CE. It embraces a wide variety of cultures and regions, from Mesopotamia and the Near East through Egypt, Greece, and Rome, to the western provinces of the Roman empire. At Penn, ancient history is an interdepartmental major and minor jointly sponsored by the Departments of Classical Studies and History and administered through the Graduate Group in Ancient History.

Requirements: The Archeological Science Minor requires a minimum of 6 course units. To declare a minor, contact the undergraduate chair.
Description: The undergraduate minor in Archaeological Science provides students with a strong background in the scientific analysis of archaeological materials. Students will be exposed to the major methods used in archaeological science and will learn to interpret scientific data derived from archaeological finds in a theoretically-informed manner. Coursework introduces students to the major analytical tools available for scientific analysis of ancient artifacts and ecofacts, while required laboratory or field experience provides direct exposure to the practice of archaeological science. In consultation with the minor advisor, students may specialize in one of three major areas: archaeobotany (the analysis of ancient plant remains), zooarchaeology (the study of ancient animal remains), or the analysis of archaeological artifacts.

Department: School of Arts and Sciences, Stuart Weitzman School of Design
Description: The Architectural History Minor is designed for students who want a broad-based introduction to the history of architecture, landscape architecture, and urbanism. The minor allows students to explore these histories from multiple disciplinary perspectives and to learn how to research and write about the built environment. It provides an especially strong basis for students interested in further graduate study in architectural history and theory, art history, historic preservation, and landscape studies.

The undergraduate minor in Architecture provides a broad introductory survey of the field of architecture in the context of a liberal arts education. It fosters an understanding of architecture as a cultural practice, a technological craft, and a profession. The program is designed for students who wish to gain a critical understanding of architecture and urbanism. The architecture minor also serves as an introduction for those students who plan to continue their education in architecture on a graduate level.

Requirements: In order to declare the minor, students must fill out the Declare/Update Field of Study Form on Path@Penn and meet with the Program Manager.
Description: The Asian American Studies (ASAM) undergraduate minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to understanding the histories, communities, and contemporary experiences of Asians in the Americas. The program highlights the creative and intellectual productions of Asian Americans, as well as their social and political struggles. Students are encouraged to develop a comparative and critical perspective on Asian American experiences by taking courses in other ethnic studies programs, as well as by taking courses that place Asian Americans in a global and diasporic context. Through a broad range of courses in ethnic studies, the humanities and the social sciences, the minor in Asian American studies provides a strong foundation for students interested in a variety of fields and careers, including law, medicine and public health, social work, education, journalism, public policy, and arts and culture.

The undergraduate minor in Bioethics, offered through the Department of Medical Ethics and Health Policy at the Perelman School of Medicine, provides an opportunity for students to systematically study the ethical, legal, and social implications of advances in biomedicine and the life sciences. The minor requires six courses in bioethics. Course offerings range from the introductory "What is Bioethics?" to more advanced seminars on topics including clinical ethics, research ethics, neuroethics, law and ethics, and global health ethics. Students have the opportunity to count courses from departments and schools across the University. The Bioethics Minor is open to all undergraduate students at the University of Pennsylvania.

Requirements: To declare a minor, students should meet with the undergraduate chair or program advisor in the sponsoring department to discuss their interests and plan a course of study. A Minor Declaration Form must be completed, signed by the minor advisor, and returned to the College Office.

Description: The undergraduate minor in biophysics is aimed at students with interests at the interface of physical and life sciences. The curriculum consists of a combination of core and elective courses in biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics, chosen to provide the breadth and depth required for this interdisciplinary field. The program is designed both for students who have a strong interest in biophysics but major in another subject, and for students who decide to major in biophysics late in their careers. It gives formal recognition to students who have made a serious commitment to biophysics.

Requirements: Students may satisfy the requirements for a Minor in Chemistry by completing six (6) course units in Chemistry as listed below. Four (4) of the six (6) courses must be numbered 200 or above. The courses used to fulfill the minor must be taken for a letter grade, not pass/fail. Lab courses cannot be counted toward the minor. Research courses may not be used to satisfy the requirements for the minor.
Description: The Chemistry Minor will provide students a strong background in the core aspects of chemistry, which could include organic, inorganic, physical, biological and materials chemistry. Chemistry is the central science and it provides the fundamental basis to understand biological processes, materials science, earth science and many other fields. This minor could serve as an excellent complement for majors in biology, physics, engineering, earth science, nursing or other majors in which a strong chemistry background will be beneficial for a future career.

Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Description: The undergraduate minor in Cinema and Media Studies offers a structured, interdisciplinary curriculum, which is organized to provide a solid grounding in the history, theory, and aesthetics of film and media. The minor is offered to all undergraduate students in the College of Arts and Sciences, Wharton, Engineering, and Nursing.

Requirements: The minor in Classical Studies consists of any six course units from the offerings of the Department of Classical Studies. A student may elect a general minor in Classical Studies or may concentrate in Greek, Latin, Ancient History, or Classical Civilization. The course requirements for the minors in Greek, Latin, Ancient History, and Classical Civilization are six courses from the respective subfield, as approved by the undergraduate chair. The requirements for the General Classical Studies minor are any six CLST courses, at least three of which must be at the 2000-level or higher. No more than one course may be at the 1000-level.
Description: The minor in Classical Studies is designed for students who want to become broadly familiar with the discipline of Classical Studies but do not have the time to devote to a full major. A student may minor in Classical Studies by taking any six courses in the department (CLST, GREK or LATN).

Cognitive science is the study of the human mind and its processes. An interdisciplinary field, it draws on many fields including psychology, linguistics, computer science, philosophy, and neuroscience. Students learn about the mind from many different levels, ranging from high-level tasks like reasoning and decision-making, to the neural mechanisms that subserve them. Research experience is an important part of the major, and students are strongly encouraged to work in a lab, whether it is for independent study course credit or on a volunteer basis. For more information please see the Cognitive Science Program website.
ScholarshipType: Need-based grants, Named Scholarships, Federal grants, State grants. A small number of merit-based music and ROTC scholarships are also available.

Description: Comparative Literature is the study of literature and culture across linguistic, national and disciplinary boundaries. The program teaches students to think critically and write cogently about a wide variety of texts, from ancient philosophy to contemporary film. Courses are cross-listed in a wide variety of departments in the humanities and social sciences. The program provides an excellent foundation for graduate study in literature, theory, and cultural studies, as well as for professional training in law, journalism, publishing, and other fields.

The minor in Computational Neuroscience (CN) is designed for students interested in the computational principles that govern how we think, perceive, and act.
